concept.name: Wyckoff accumulation
concept.definition: The phase of the Wyckoff price cycle in which large interests buy a sizeable position inside a trading range after a downtrend, halting the decline and building the 'cause' for a later markup. It is a hypothesized pattern recognized through characteristic events and phases, not a guaranteed bottom formation.
concept.intuition: Smart money fills its shopping cart quietly while everyone else is still bearish; the price stops falling because every selloff gets absorbed.
concept.mechanics: An accumulation trading range typically shows preliminary support, a selling climax, an automatic rally, and secondary tests (Phase A); a cause-building stretch of back-and-forth institutional buying (Phase B); a decisive test of remaining supply such as a spring (Phase C); signs of strength with higher lows (Phase D); and departure from the range as demand takes control (Phase E). Volume tends to expand on rallies and contract on reactions as supply is absorbed.
concept.failure_modes: Ranges that look like accumulation can fail and resolve downward, especially if a spring is not followed by strength or if the broad market is falling; labeling is retrospective and a 'base' can simply be a redistribution range in disguise.
concept.misconceptions: Accumulation does not require a spring or any single schematic to match exactly, and a completed-looking accumulation does not guarantee a markup of a particular size.
concept.example: After a 40% decline, a stock churns sideways for six months on declining reaction volume; a brief dip below the range low on light volume (spring) is followed by a wide-spread rally (SOS), which the analyst reads as completed accumulation.

citations.source: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett)
